title: The hillside water survey
paragraphs: When the school science club began mapping springs above Hillview village, its members expected a short walk. Their teacher, Ms Tan, warned them that recent rain had made the paths slippery. She asked each pair to carry a compass and reminded them to keep it dry. Before leaving, Ben counted the six students assigned to his group, and the class divided the route {{1}} three sections.

The first group reached the lower spring without difficulty. The water looked clear, {{2}} Aisha still collected a sample for testing. She labelled the bottle immediately so that it would not be confused {{3}} samples from the other springs.

Farther uphill, Ben's group found a narrow wooden bridge. It had been repaired the previous month, but one plank had worked {{4}} in the rain. Rather {{5}} step on it, Ben asked the group to cross beside the handrail one person at a time. Once everyone was safely across, he counted the group {{6}} before they continued.

At the upper spring, a dark cloud hid the sun, and several students wanted to rush their measurements. Ms Tan insisted that the data would be useless {{7}} every group used the same method. The students therefore waited for the rain to pass and repeated the depth reading twice. By the time the sun appeared, the wind {{8}} fallen and the surface was calm enough for a reliable final reading.

Back at school, the three groups compared their maps, labels and measurements. Aisha noticed that the clearest water had not come from the highest spring, while Ben's careful headcount explained why the class returned together. The survey took longer than expected, yet the students trusted the record because each decision could be checked.
